Period: Second Temple period, especially the first century AD
Origin: The Sanhedrin was the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, rooted in the biblical pattern of elders judging the people and developed under Persian, Greek, and Roman rule into a court of seventy-one under the high priest. Under Rome its powers were real but limited: it governed religious life and local affairs, while capital punishment required the Roman governor.
Beliefs: The council was not a party with one theology. It mixed Sadducean chief priests and elders with Pharisaic scribes, so its members disagreed sharply — notably over the resurrection — and decisions came from debate and majority vote rather than shared doctrine.
Practices: It met in Jerusalem, tried religious and civil cases, issued rulings, sent messengers, and policed the Temple. Its sessions could be formal or hurried, and the Gospel accounts show it acting at night in Jesus' case, a detail that has long been debated by scholars.
Role: The Sanhedrin was the highest Jewish authority most Jews would ever meet: court, council, and senate in one. Ordinary people looked to it for justice and for the boundaries of faithful life, and Rome tolerated it as the instrument of local self-government.
RelationshipToJesus: The Sanhedrin condemned Jesus after a night hearing and handed him to Pilate, pressing for crucifixion. It then tried the apostles, imprisoned and flogged them, and stoned Stephen. Yet its own members were divided: Nicodemus urged a fair hearing, Joseph of Arimathea dissented, and Gamaliel — named in Acts though he has no profile on this site — advised restraint.
KeyMembers: Caiaphas; Annas; Nicodemus; Joseph of Arimathea
Summary: The Sanhedrin was Jerusalem's supreme council of seventy-one — chief priests, elders, and scribes under the high priest — the court that judged Jesus and then tried to silence his apostles, while remaining deeply divided within itself.
RelatedTopics: Leadership; Justice; Biblical Authority; Persecution; Church History
